scenes.heading: Data Skew: Detection & Salting
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Data Skew: Detection & Salting and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: What skew is
items: A few keys hold most of the rows
scenes.narration: Data skew occurs when a small number of keys carry a disproportionate share of the rows. After a shuffle, all rows for a hot key land in one partition, so that partition's task runs far longer than the others. These straggler tasks stretch out the stage and can even exhaust memory, while the rest of the cluster sits idle.

scenes.heading: Detecting skew
steps: Stage runs long with one slow task
Max task time ≫ median in UI
scenes.narration: You usually detect skew in the Stages tab when one task lags far behind the rest and the maximum task time dwarfs the median. To confirm, you count rows per key and look for a handful of keys with enormous counts. That distribution, a few giant keys among many small ones, is the fingerprint of skew. Once confirmed, salting is the classic remedy.

scenes.code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, concat_ws, lit, rand, floor

N = 16  # salt buckets
fact = fact.withColumn("salt", floor(rand() * N))
fact = fact.withColumn("skey", concat_ws("_", col("key"), col("salt")))

dim_exploded = dim.crossJoin(spark.range(N).withColumnRenamed("id", "salt"))
dim_exploded = dim_exploded.withColumn("skey", concat_ws("_", col("key"), col("salt")))

joined = fact.join(dim_exploded, "skey").drop("salt", "skey")
scenes.heading: Salting a skewed join
scenes.narration: Salting spreads a hot key across multiple buckets so no single partition is overloaded. We append a random salt from zero to fifteen to the fact table's key, and we replicate every dimension row across all sixteen salt values so matches still find each other. Joining on the salted key distributes the hot key's rows over sixteen partitions instead of one. We then drop the helper columns to restore the original shape.

scenes.heading: Salting vs AQE skew join
scenes.narration: Manual salting gives you precise control and works on any version, at the cost of extra code and care to keep matches aligned. AQE's skew-join handling detects oversized partitions at runtime and splits them automatically, with no code changes, on Spark three and later. Enabling AQE first is often the right move, reserving manual salting for cases AQE cannot fully solve.

scenes.heading: Other skew remedies
items: Broadcast the small side to avoid the shuffle
Filter out or handle null/default hot keys
Isolate hot keys and union results
scenes.narration: Salting is not the only tool against skew. If the other side is small, broadcasting it sidesteps the shuffle entirely and with it the skew. Often a single sentinel value like null or zero is the hot key, so filtering or special-casing it removes the imbalance. You can also split hot keys into their own job and union the results back.

scenes.text: Enable AQE skew handling first; salt only if that isn't enough.
scenes.narration: Salting is powerful but invasive, so try the automatic path before hand-rolling salt keys and replicated dimensions.
